FOREWORD 
This Indian Standard (Part 44) (Second Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the 
draft finalized by the Water Quality Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 


Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) is the most important parameter to determine the degree of pollution in 
lakes and streams at any time and their self-purification capacities, assess the biodegradable organic load of the 
wastewaters for design of wastewater management system and thereafter to evaluate the efficiency of the same. 
As per definition BOD of a sample is defined as the amount of oxygen required by the micro-organisms to oxidise 
the organic matter by aerobic microbial decomposition to stable inorganic forms at some standard time and 
temperature. 


Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) test uses standard laboratory procedures to determine the relative oxygen 
requirements of waters, wastewaters, effluents, etc. There are a number of variations to the oxygen demand test 
prescribed in this standard. These include using shorter or longer incubation periods, higher temperatures, etc. 


In a tropical country like India, the temperature of surface water in rivers, lakes, etc., vary from 20 °C to 35 °C in 
different seasons and in different parts of the country. The average aquatic temperature in our country is around 
27 °C . Therefore the incubation temperature has been set at 27 °C and the incubation period as 3 days with an 
assumption that most of the carbonaceous organic demand is satisfied during this period. 


The Technical Committee responsible for formulation of IS 2488 (Part 1): 1966 Methods of sampling and test for 
industrial effluents, Part 1 and IS 3025 : 1964 ‘Methods of sampling and test (physical and chemical) for water 
used in industry’ decided to revise the standard and publish it in separate parts. This standard superseded 12 of 
IS 2488 (Part 1) : 1966 Methods of sampling and test for industrial effluents, Part 1 and 53 of IS 3025 : 1964 
Methods of sampling and test (physical and chemical) for water used in industry and was one among the 
different parts published under IS 3025 series of standards. The first revision of this standard was published in 
1986. 


In this second revision the following major modifications have been made: 

a) Amendment No. | has been incorporated; and 

b) Test procedure (Clause 9) has been modified. 
In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from Standard Methods for 
Examination of Water and Wastewater published by American Public Health Association, Washington, USA, 
23" edition. 
The composition of the committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is listed in Annex A. 
In reporting the results of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 


calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 2022 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical 
values (second revision)’. 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023 


Indian Standard 


METHODS OF SAMPLING AND TEST (PHYSICAL 


AND CHEMICAL) FOR WATER AND WASTEWATER 
PART 44 BIOCHEMICAL OXYGEN DEMAND (BOD) 


(Second Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard (Part 44) prescribes oxygen depletion 
method based on _ bio-assay procedure for 
measurement of biochemical oxygen demand. 


2 REFERENCES 


The following standards listed below contain 
provisions which through reference in this text 
constitute provisions of this standard. At the time of 
publications, the editions indicated were valid. All 
standards are subject to revision and parties to 
agreements based on this standard are encouraged to 
investigate the possibility of applying the most 
recent editions of the standards listed below:

3 TERMINOLOGY 


For the purpose of this standard, definitions given in 
IS 7022 (Part 1) and IS 7022 (Part 2) shall apply. 


4 SAMPLING AND PRESERVATION 


Sampling and sample preservation shall be 
done as prescribed in IS 17614 (Part 1) and 
IS 17614 (Part 2). 


5 PRINCIPLE 


5.1 The biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) test is 
based on mainly bio-assay procedure which 
measures the dissolved oxygen consumed by 
micro-organisms while assimilating and oxidizing 
the organic matter under aerobic conditions. 


5.2 The standard test condition includes incubating 
the sample in an air tight bottle, in dark at as 
specified temperature for specific time. 


6 APPARATUS 


6.1 Incubation Bottles 


6.1.1 300 ml capacity narrow neck special BOD 
bottles with planed mouth with ground glass 
stoppers. New bottles should be cleaned with 
5 N hydrochloric acid or sulphuric acid followed by 
rinsing with distilled water. In normal use, bottles 
once used for Winklers procedure should only be 
rinsed with tap water followed by distilled water. 


6.1.2 During incubation (if incubator is used) to 
ensure proper sealing, time to time, add water to the 
flared mouth of the bottle. 


6.2 Water Bath or Air Incubator 


Air incubation with thermostatically controlled 
27 °C + 1 °C. Avoid light to prevent possibility of 
photosynthetic production of oxygen. 


NOTE — Thermostatically controlled at 27 °C + 1 °C 
water bath with continuous stirring may be preferred. 


7 REAGENTS 
7.1 Phosphate Buffer Solution 


Dissolve 8.5 g potassium di-hydrogen phosphate 
(KH2PO,), 21.75 g potassium hydrogen phosphate 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023 


(K2HPOs,), 33.4 g disodium hydrogen phosphate 
(Na2HPO,.7H2O) and 1.7 g ammonium chloride 
(NH,Cl) in about 500 ml distilled water and dilute to 
1 litre. pH of the solution should be around 
7.2 without any further adjustment. 


7.2 Magnesium Sulphate Solution 


Dissolve 22.5 g magnesium sulphate 
(MgSO4.7H20) in distilled water and dilute to 1 litre. 


7.3 Calcium Chloride Solution 


Dissolve 27.5 g calcium chloride in distilled water 
and dilute to 1 litre. 


7.4 Ferric Chloride Solution 


Dissolve 0.25 g hydrated ferric chloride 
(FeCl3.6H20) in distilled water and dilute to 1 litre. 


7.5 Acid and Alkali Solution 


1 N sodium hydroxide and 1 N sulphuric acid for 
neutralization of samples. 


NOTE — Any of the above solutions showing any sign of 
biological growth may be discarded. 


7.6 Glucose-Glutamic Acid (GGA) Solution 


Dry reagent grade glucose and reagent grade 
glutamic acid at 103 °C for 1 h. Add 150 mg of 
glucose and 150 mg of glutamic acid to distilled 
water and dilute to 1 litre. Prepare fresh immediately 
before use. 


7.7 Other Reagents for Dissolved Oxygen 
Measurement 


7.7.1 Manganous Sulphate Solution 


Dissolve manganese sulphate (480 g of 
MnS0O4.4H20 or 400 g of MnSO4.2H20 or 364 g of 
MnSO,.H2O) in freshly boiled and cooled water, 
filter and make up to 1 000 ml. The solution should 
not give blue colour by addition of acidified 
potassium iodide solution and starch. 


7.7.2 Alkali-Ilodide Azide-Reagent 


Dissolve 500 g of sodium hydroxide 
(or 700 g of potassium hydroxide) and 135 g of 
sodium iodide (or 150 g of potassium iodide) in 
freshly boiled and cooled water and dilute tol litre. 


Dissolve 10 gm of sodium azide in 40 ml of distilled 
water and add this with constant stirring to the cool 
alkaline iodide solution. 


7.7.3 Sulphuric Acid, Concentrated 
7.7.4 Starch Indicator 


Dissolve 2 g of starch and 0.2 g of salicylic acid as 
preservative, in 100 ml of hot distilled water. 


7.7.5 Sodium Thiosulphate Stock Solution 


Dissolve approximately 25 g of sodium thiosulphate 
(Na2S203.5H20) in boiled distilled water and make 
up to 1 000 ml. Add 1 g of sodium hydroxide to 
preserve it. 


7.7.6 Standard Sodium Thiosulphate Solution 


Dissolve 250 ml of stock solution (7.7.5) in boiled 
distilled water and make up to 1 litre and standardize 
sodium thiosulphate against known standard before 
use. 


7.7.7 Potassium Dichromate Solution, K2Cr2Oz, 
0.025 N 


Dissolve 1.225 9 gm of K2Cr207 (previously dried at 
150 °C for 2 h) in distilled water and dilute to 1 litre. 


7.7.8 Potassium Iodate Solution, 0.025 N 


Dissolve 0.892 5 gm. of KIO3 (dried at 120 °C to 
140 °C) in distilled water and dilute to 1 litre. 


8 INTERFERENCES 


Oxidizing agents give positive interferences and 
reducing agents give negative interferences. Nitrite 
interference is removed by adding sodium azide to 
alkaline iodide solution. 


9 PROCEDURE 
9.1 Preparation of Dilution Water 


Aerate the required volume of distilled water in a 
container by bubbling compressed air for 8 h to 
12 h to attain dissolved oxygen saturation. Let it 
stabilize for 4 h at room temperature (around 27 °C). 
Add 1 ml each of phosphate buffer solution, 
magnesium sulphate solution, calcium chloride 
solution and ferric chloride solution before aerating 
or may be added alternately at the time of preparing 
the sample dilutions. 


9.2 Dilution Water Check 


With each batch of dilution water, incubate at least 
two or more bottles of dilution water containing 
nutrient, mineral and buffer solutions without seed 
to verify the quality of water. One set of Dilution 


water checks must be analyzed with each batch of 
samples. The dilution water blank serves as a check 
on the quality of unseeded dilution water and 
cleanliness of incubation bottles. Determine initial 
and final Dissolved Oxygen (DO) for each bottle and 
average the results. The average DO uptake in 3 days 
must not be greater than 0.2 mg/l and preferably 
< 0.1 mg/l before making seed corrections. If 
average dilution water blank is greater than 
0.2 mg/l, record the data and clearly identify such 
samples in data records 


9.3 Addition of Seed to Dilution Water 


Use treated sewage or commercially available 
microbial seed mixture for seeding purposes. 


When treated sewage is not available, use 
supernatant from domestic waste water after settling 
at room temperature for at least 1 h but not longer 
than 36 h. The preferred seed is effluent or mixed 
liquor from a biological treatment system processing 
the waste. 


NOTE — Seeding’s not required for domestic sewage or 
surface water samples. 


The DO uptake attributable to the seed added to each 
BOD bottle generally should be between 
0.6 mg/l and 1.0 mg/l but the amount of seed added 
should be adjusted from this range to that required 
to provide glucose-glutamic acid (GGA) check 
results of 198 mg/l + 30.5 mg/l. For example, if 1 ml 
of seed suspension is required to achieve 
198 mg/l + 30.5 mg/l BOD in the glucose-glutamic 
acid check, then add 1 ml of seed suspension in each 
sample bottle. 


9.4 Neutralization 

Neutralize the sample to pH around 7.0 using alkali 
or acid of such strength that the quantity of reagent 
does not dilute the sample by more than 0.5 percent. 
9.5 Sample Volume and Dilution Techniques 


Four types of dilutions were suggested for use: 


9.5.1 Method I Dilutions Based on Expected BOD 
and COD Values 


On the basis of Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD), 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023 


determine expected BOD. Use the following 
formula for calculating sample volume: 


Sample volume in ml, per | dilution = 


——— x 1 000 
expected BOD 


For keeping 2 dilutions take X = 2.5 and 4.0 
For single dilution take X = 3.0 or 3.5. 


9.5.2 Method 2 Direct Dilution if the Sources are 
Known 


If unknown concentrations is given the following 
idea can be used: 


a) Strong effluents 0.1 percent to | percent; 

b) Raw or settled waste 1 percent to 5 percent; 

c) Biologically treated water 5 percent to 
25 percent; and 

d) River water/surface waters 25 percent to 
100 percent. 


9.5.3 Method 3 Percent Dilution of Sample in 1 litre 
Measuring Cylinders and Siphoning Techniques 


Fill a 1 litre volumetric flask with approximately 
300 ml dilution water as prepared. Add the specific 
volume of sample in it as per dilution technique 
given in Table 1. If the dilution water is not feeded 
with nutrients during aeration, then add 1 ml each of 
phosphate buffer solution, magnesium sulphate 
solution, calcium chloride solution and ferric 
chloride solution one by one in the volumetric flask. 
If the sample requires seeding, add the requisite 
volume of seed which meets the GGA check of 
198 °C + 30.5 °C as mentioned in Table 2 and dilute 
to the mark with the dilution water by siphoning 
from the dilution water container. Mix well. Rinse 
three BOD bottles with the diluted sample and fill 
up these bottles with the diluted sample by siphoning 
from the volumetric flask. Stopper the bottles 
immediately after removing the air bubbles. Repeat 
the same process for other dilutions of the sample. 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023

NOTE — The dilutions taken for BOD should result in a residual DO of at least 1 mg/l and a DO uptake of at least 2 mg/l after 3 


days’ incubation. 


9.5.4 Method for Direct Pipetting the Samples into 
BOD Bottles if Large Number of Samples are 
Handled 


Samples of natural surface water bodies like River, 
Lake and marine, generally do not require seeding 
and dilution due to naturally available 
microbiological population and low BOD values. 
For such samples which are likely to have BOD less 
than 5 mg/l, BOD determination may be carried out 
as such (100 percent) without any dilution. 


9.6 Use of Seed Control 


For preparing a seed control, fill up a 1 litre 
volumetric flask partly with the dilution water, add 
20 ml of seed (2 percent of freshly collected or 
stabilised settled sewage) in it and 1 ml each of the 


nutrients and fill up to the mark with the dilution 
water. The volume of seed added may vary 
depending on the quality of seed used. 


9.7 Sealing Bottles 


Completely fill each bottle by adding enough 
dilution water so that insertion of stopper leaves no 
bubbles in the bottle. Mix sample by turning bottle 
manually several times. As a precaution against 
drawing air into the BOD bottles during incubation, 
use a water seal. Obtain satisfactory water seals by 
inverting bottles in a water bath or by adding water 
to the flared mouth of the BOD bottles. During 
incubation (if incubator is used), in order to ensure 
proper sealing, add water to the flared mouth of the 
bottle from time to time. 


9.8 Sample Incubation 


Incubate at 27 °C + 1 °C the stoppered and sealed 
BOD bottles containing desired dilutions, seed 
controls, dilution water blanks and GGA checks. 
Exclude light to avoid algae growth in bottles during 
incubation. 


9.9 Standardisation of Sodium Thiosulphate 
Solution using Potassium Iodate/Potassium 
Dichromate Solution 


Take 25 ml of potassium iodate solution 
(0.025 N) or 25 ml of potassium dichromate solution 
(0.025 N) in a 250 ml. glass-stoppered conical flask 
and add 5 ml concentrated H2SOxz to it. Add 1 gm 
KI to it and keep it in the dark for a few min. Then 
titrate this against Na2S2O3 solution adding starch 
towards the end of titration, when a pale straw colour 
appears. Continue titration till the solution becomes 
colourless. Determine the strength of sodium 
thiosulphate solution using the normality equation. 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023 


9.10 Determination of Initial Dissolved Oxygen 
(DO) 


Determine initial DO for one bottle and keep 
two bottles with samples for incubation at 
27 °C + 1 °C for 3 days. 


NOTE — DO shall be determined as per IS 3025 (Part 38). 
9.11 Determination of Final DO 


After 3 days incubation at 27 °C + 1 °C, determine 
final DO in incubated bottles. 


NOTE — DO shall be determined as per IS 3025 (Part 38). 
10 CALCULATION 


For each test bottle having 2.0 mg/l Min DO 
depletion and at least 1.0 mg/l residual DO, calculate 
BOD as follows: 


10.1 When Sample is Undiluted and Direct 
Sample is Used for Fresh Surface Waters/Rivers 
and Less Than 5 mg/l 


BOD, mg/l = DO, in mg/l before incubation — 
DO, in mg/l after incubation after 3 days 


10.2 When Dilution Water is not Seeded but 
Suitable Volume of Sample is Taken in Less 
Polluted Waters 


D,—-D2 


BOD, mg/l = x 1 000 


10.3 When Dilution Water is Seeded 


D,—D2)—-{(B,—-B 
BOD, mg/l = oe. 1000 


where 
D: = initial DO of sample in mg/l; 
D2 = DO of sample after incubation in mg/l; 


Bı = DO of seed control before incubation in 
mg/l; 


B2 = DO of seed control after incubation in mg/l; 


f = ratio of seed in diluted sample to seed in 
control; [volume (ml) of seed in diluted 
sample/volume of seed in seed control]; 
and 


V = sample volume (in ml). 


NOTE — f may be used only when seed correction is to be 
applied. 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023 


11 GLUCOSE GLUTAMIC ACID CHECK 


BOD being a bioassay test, is greatly influenced by 
factors like toxicants, poor seeding, etc. For 
periodical checking of these factors, use a mixture of 
150 mg/l glucose and 150 mg/l glutamic acid as a 
standard check solution. Take five sets of 2 percent 
Glucose-glutamic acid solutions for the check. Add 
1 ml, 2 ml, 3 ml, 4 ml and 5 ml seed in the 1 litre 
volumetric flasks containing the 2 percent GGA 
solutions respectively along with the nutrients and 
make up the volume with the dilution water. 
Determine the 3 days 27 °C BOD of 2 percent 
dilution of the glucose-glutamic acid standard check 


solutions as in 9. If the average BOD value of 
the check solutions is outside the range of 
198 mg/l + 30.5 mg/l, reject any BOD 
determinations made with the seed and dilution 
water and seek the cause of the problem. 


12 EXPRESSION OF RESULTS 


BOD is expressed as mg/l, 3 days at 27 °C as given 
in 10 and round off the values as follows: 


a) Oto 10 up to first decimal; and 
b) Above 10— whole number. 


IS 3025 (Part 44) : 2023

Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed
